## 1. The subdomain list

> Here are the 7 subdomains under `multimodal`. What is missing? What is a distinction nobody in your field actually makes? What are we calling by the wrong name?

(03 §12.2, ask 1.) The family: Benchmarks whose scored quantity is the relation between two or more modalities.

- Included: Tag this as PRIMARY if success requires crossing between modalities -- answering in language about an image, binding an expression to a region, retrieving across modalities, or generating in one modality from another such that the correspondence is what is scored.
- Excluded: Do NOT tag this if the benchmark is scored wholly inside one modality, which is \`vision\` or \`audio-speech\`. The boundary is the correspondence: VQA scores whether the answer matches the image, whereas image restoration scores the image alone.

### 2.1 MMMU-Pro (mmmu-pro)

`data/benchmarks/multimodal/mmmu-pro.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*MMMU's image-dependent questions with ten options and a vision-only setting that puts the question inside the image.*

A more robust revision of MMMU by the MMMU team (ACL 2025). Four open text-only LLMs answered MMMU's questions without their images, ten times each, and every question that at least three of them answered correctly in most trials was removed; 1,800 of the remaining questions were sampled evenly across MMMU's 30 subjects. Each question's options were then augmented from four to (usually) ten, proposed with GPT-4o and reviewed by human experts, who also removed 70 questions, leaving 1,730. A vision-only setting presents the same 1,730 questions as screenshots or photos that annotators took of a display, with varied backgrounds and fonts and no text fed to the model. The headline score is accuracy averaged over the standard ten-option setting and the vision setting; a four-option standard setting is reported for comparison only. The paper runs every model with a direct and a chain-of-thought prompt and reports the higher. The maintainers' leaderboard, shared with MMMU, lists their own runs beside results provided by model developers, and human-expert bands estimated from MMMU's human evaluation. Items and answers are public on Hugging Face, where the maintainers date the fixes they make.

#### mmmu-pro · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary multimodal/visual-qa; secondary general-intelligence/multi-subject-knowledge-exams · [S2][mmmu-pro-s2]
  - why: Every scored item is a question whose answer depends on its image. The first construction step removes the MMMU questions that text-only models answer, and the vision setting moves the question itself into the image. What is scored is an answer chosen in language against an image, which is the relation vision's exclusion test hands to multimodal and multimodal's inclusion test takes ("answering in language about an image"); nothing recovered from the image is scored on its own. The breadth across MMMU's 30 subjects is recorded as the secondary leaf, because general-intelligence's exclusion sends a multi-subject exam whose every item needs the image to multimodal (ADR-0015), and visual-qa's not\_to\_be\_confused\_with keeps such an exam in visual-qa.
  > (1) filtering out questions answerable by text-only models, (2) augmenting candidate options, and (3) introducing a vision-only input setting where questions are embedded within images
- `capability` = perception · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: Every item needs its image, and in the vision setting the question and its options must also be recovered from a screenshot or photo before anything else can happen.
  > In this setting, the model is presented with a question embedded within a screenshot or photo, without any text explicitly fed into the model
- `capability` = knowledge-recall · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: The protocol supplies the question, its images and its options only; the college-level subject knowledge the answer needs is what the model brings, as in MMMU.
  > to evaluate multimodal AI models on college-level tasks that require subject-specific knowledge and deliberate reasoning
- `capability` = context-integration · [S2][mmmu-pro-s2]
  - why: The filter keeps only questions whose answer depends on the supplied image, removing those that text-only LLMs answered without it, so the score tests whether the image was used.
  > filtering out questions answerable by text-only models
- `evaluation_method` = multiple-choice · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: The model picks one lettered option. The standard and vision settings have up to ten options per question, usually ten, so chance is about 0.10; the leaderboard's Random Choice row scores 12.6 overall. Accuracy is computed per setting, and the headline averages the standard ten-option setting and the vision setting. The direct prompt asks for the option letter, and the CoT prompt for reasoning that ends in an answer line, so the prompt mode is a condition of every number.
  > The overall performance score for MMMU-Pro is calculated as the average of scores from settings (2) and (3)
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: Models are prompted zero-shot, without tools, with an instruction to answer a multiple-choice question. The paper runs each model with a direct and a chain-of-thought prompt and keeps the higher score.
  > We evaluate the models with both Direct and CoT prompts (as shown in Appendix A), and report the higher ones in the overall results

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `vision/document-understanding` · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: The vision setting's inputs are screenshots and photos of question pages, so text must be read from the image, but the score is the option chosen, not extracted structure or text. The paper argues that reading is not what the setting tests, and an OCR-first prompt did not change results. The images are rendered exam questions rather than forms, tables or reports (see review\_checks).
  > requiring models to not only recognize text but also understand its context
- `domain` not `vision/ocr-handwriting` · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: The paper measures OCR accuracy (Levenshtein similarity of the extracted question text) as an analysis, but no benchmark setting scores a transcription.
  > explicitly asking the model to first extract the question and then solve it
- `domain` not `multimodal/chart-diagram-understanding` · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: Charts and diagrams are among MMMU's 30 image types, but no setting or score isolates them, and the benchmark's changes concern the image-text relation for every image type.
  > featuring 30 diverse image types such as charts, diagrams, maps, and chemical structures
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: The vision setting re-presents the same questions in photos and screenshots with varied backgrounds and fonts, scored as its own condition, but the protocol is zero-shot and defines no distribution the system was fitted to. The setting is the benchmark's construct, reading text and image together, not a held-out input condition.
  > This process involves varying the backgrounds, font styles, and font sizes
- `capability` not `adversarial-robustness` · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: "Robust" describes the benchmark. The filter removes questions that text-only LLMs answer, chosen against shortcuts in the item set, not inputs chosen to defeat the system under test.
  > The dataset may still contain subtle statistical shortcuts that models can exploit
- `designed_for_subjects` not `human-expert` · [S1][mmmu-pro-s1]
  - why: The leaderboard's three Human Expert rows were not produced under MMMU-Pro's protocol. The paper approximates them from MMMU's human evaluation data, guessing among the augmented options where an expert wrote no solution.
  > we develop an approach to approximate human expert performance based on the original MMMU human evaluation data

**Open review checks** (8):

1. (field `domain.secondary`) The vision setting's images are screenshots and photos of question pages. vision/document-understanding's not\_to\_be\_confused\_with makes it secondary for a document-image benchmark posed as questions; it was rejected here because the images are rendered exam questions rather than documents, which a reviewer may read differently.
2. (field `activity`) activity unknown or accepting-submissions: 49 author-provided MMMU-Pro rows, the newest dated 2026-07-01, show results still reaching the board, but no source states a route. The same script-written date bears on MMMU's entry, whose activity basis reads the static "Last updated: 09/05/2025". · [S8][mmmu-pro-s8]
   > Last updated: 09/05/2025
3. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle active or under-revision. Fixes keep arriving (2026-05-30, 2026-07-10, twice on 2026-10-04), each announced as done, with nothing announced as pending. · [S9][mmmu-pro-s9]
   > \[2026-05-30\] Fixed the option augmentation issue in Vision and Standard (10 options) settings.
4. (field `governance.submission_process`) self-reported assumes developers send their numbers. Many author-provided rows link to the developer's announcement (GPT-5.4 links an OpenAI page), so the maintainers may copy published numbers instead, which no submission\_process term describes exactly.
5. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark rests on four MMMU-Pro authors co-authoring MAmmoTH-VL, whose MMMU-Pro row is author-provided; the maintainers did not enter a system as the MMMU team. · [S10][mmmu-pro-s10]
   > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
6. (field `capability`) knowledge-recall and context-integration are both assigned, each term's not\_to\_be\_confused\_with pointing at the other. The image is supplied and determines the answer; the subject knowledge is not supplied.
7. (field `lineage`) lineage subset\_of mmmu. The items are MMMU questions with rewritten options and a new rendering, not unchanged MMMU items; role variant without subset\_of may fit better.
8. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium against MMMU's high, on largely the same questions. MMMU's evidence is its released test answers; MMMU-Pro's options and vision images are its own.

### 2.2 TextVQA (textvqa)

`data/benchmarks/multimodal/textvqa.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-10 · last verified 2026-11-10

*45,336 questions on Open Images photos answerable only by reading their text, scored by VQA accuracy.*

Visual question answering that needs reading. Crowd workers were shown Open Images photographs from categories likely to contain text (billboards, traffic signs, whiteboards) and asked for questions that cannot be answered without reading the text in the image; ten other workers answered each one. The 45,336 questions on 28,408 images are split into 34,602 training, 5,000 validation and 5,734 test questions, the test images drawn from Open Images' own test set. Answers are open-ended, usually one or two words, a brand, a name, a number or a time, and are often copied from the scene text, though some must be inferred from it. The dataset ships OCR tokens from the Rosetta system with every image; v0.5.1 (March 2020) replaced those tokens and changed nothing else. The score is VQA accuracy, VQA v2's consensus measure: an answer counts in full when at least three of the human answers match it. Test answers are withheld and scored on EvalAI, where a standing test-standard leaderboard has remained open since the 2021 challenge. The release paper's LoRRA model, which adds an OCR module and a copy mechanism to a VQA network, reached 26.56% on validation against 85.01% for humans; the leaderboard's top row is 84.22, and current vision-language models report validation accuracy in their technical reports.

#### textvqa · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary multimodal/visual-qa; secondary vision/ocr-handwriting · [S2][textvqa-s2]
  - why: Each item is a natural-language question about a photograph, and the score is whether the free-form answer matches the human answers to that question about that image. The paper's question-only and image-only baselines reach 8.09% and 6.29%, so neither modality alone carries the score and the question-image correspondence is what is measured; multimodal's inclusion test ("answering in language about an image") and vision's exclusion test both send it here, and visual-qa is the leaf for questions answered about an image. vision/ocr-handwriting is secondary because reading the scene text is the skill the benchmark was built to test and many answers are that text copied out of the image (30.6% of validation answers are among the Rosetta tokens), but no transcription is scored, so it cannot be the primary.
  > Question only (Q) and Image only (I) baseline get 8.09% and 6.29% validation accuracies, respectively
- `capability` = perception · [S2][textvqa-s2]
  - why: The answer depends on text recovered from the image itself, often rotated, partly occluded or stylised; the paper's examples need hidden characters inferred and rotated text read, and its OCR upper bound is far under human accuracy.
  > Questions require inferring hidden characters
- `capability` = context-integration · [S2][textvqa-s2]
  - why: The image the protocol supplies holds the answer. Question writers were told that answering must require reading the image's text, and the answer is taken or inferred from that text rather than from what the system already knows.
  > Please ensure that answering the question requires reading of the text in the image.
- `evaluation_method` = reference-metric · [S3][textvqa-s3]
  - why: VQA accuracy is a fixed formula over ten human reference answers. After normalisation the predicted answer earns min(1, n/3), where n is how many of the other nine answers match it, averaged over the ten leave-one-out sets, so an answer two annotators gave earns partial credit. It is a reference similarity computed by formula, not a learned model and not specific to a scientific field.
  > acc = min(1, float(len(matching\_answers)) / 3)
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S2][textvqa-s2]
  - why: The dataset ships a 34,602-question training split, and the release paper's entrants are VQA networks (Pythia, BAN) with and without its LoRRA reading module, trained on that split and selected on validation; the challenges' starter code trains such models. Reading scene text is a general perception task, not a discipline.
  > We train all of our models for 24000 iterations

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `vision/document-understanding` · [S2][textvqa-s2]
  - why: The images are photographs of everyday scenes (signs, jerseys, clocks, labels), not document pages, and no layout, form or table structure is extracted or scored.
  > We use Open Images v3 dataset \[27\] as the source of our images.
- `capability` not `knowledge-recall` · [S2][textvqa-s2]
  - why: Some answers are inferred or paraphrased from the text (a team name read from a jersey, an aircraft type from its markings) and may lean on world knowledge, but the questions were written so that the text in the image decides the answer.
  > It is OK if the answer cannot be directly copied from the text but needs to be inferred or paraphrased.
- `capability` not `spatial-reasoning` · [S2][textvqa-s2]
  - why: Many questions locate the text they ask about ("on the top left", "the player on the right"), but position only selects which text to read; no score isolates spatial judgement.
  > Workers often form questions which are longer to disambiguate the response
- `evaluation_method` not `exact-match` · [S4][textvqa-s4]
  - why: Each comparison is an exact string match after normalisation, but exact-match's exclusion test rules it out where partial credit is available, and VQA accuracy gives a third or two thirds of a point to answers fewer than three annotators gave.
  > We use the same metric as VQA v2 which is robust to inter-human variability in phrasing the answers.

### 2.3 VQA (vqa)

`data/benchmarks/multimodal/vqa.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-10 · last verified 2026-11-10

*Open-ended questions about COCO images, each answered by ten people and scored by agreement with them.*

Free-form, open-ended questions about images, written by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, three per image, and answered by ten workers each. v1.0 (October 2015) has 614,163 questions on 204,721 COCO images and 150,000 on 50,000 clipart abstract scenes made for the dataset, with two tasks: open-ended, and multiple-choice among 18 candidates. v2.0 (April 2017) balances the real-image set: for almost every question a second, similar COCO image was collected on which the answer differs, which gives 1,105,904 questions and weakens the answers a model can guess from the question alone. v2.0 has the open-ended task only. Answers are mostly one word, and an answer scores min(n/3, 1), where n is how many of the ten annotators gave it, averaged over the ten sets of nine. The real-image test set is split, following COCO, into test-dev for development, test-standard for reported results and a public leaderboard, test-challenge for the annual challenge's winners and a never-revealed test-reserve; test answers are withheld and scored on EvalAI. Six challenges ran at CVPR from 2016 to 2021, and the test-standard leaderboard still takes submissions: 559 rows, the newest dated 2026-11-03.

#### vqa · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary multimodal/visual-qa · [S3][vqa-s3]
  - why: Each item is a natural-language question about an image, and the score is whether the answer in language agrees with the answers of people who saw the image, so the question-image-answer relation is what is scored, which is multimodal's inclusion test ("answering in language about an image"). vision's exclusion test sends a question answered about an image to multimodal, and multimodal's own exclusion test names VQA as its example of a scored correspondence. The questions were collected to need the image, and v2.0 pairs each question with two images whose answers differ, so the question alone does not decide the answer. visual-qa is the leaf whose definition this is.
  > Importantly, questions should also require the image to correctly answer and not be answerable using just commonsense information
- `capability` = perception · [S4][vqa-s4]
  - why: The answer has to be recovered from the image (objects, attributes, counts, activities, scene context), and v2.0 was built so that the same question has different answers on two similar images; the v2.0 paper finds that models trained on v1.0 lean on language priors and lose accuracy on the balanced set.
  > All models perform significantly worse on our balanced dataset, suggesting that these models have indeed learned to exploit language priors.
- `evaluation_method` = reference-metric · [S3][vqa-s3]
  - why: Each answer is normalised and matched exactly against the ten human answers to the question, and the score is the fixed formula min(n/3, 1) over the number n of matching annotators, averaged over the ten sets of nine annotators. That is partial credit by a fixed formula against several references, which exact-match's exclusion test (no partial credit) leaves out; the vocabulary has no term for consensus scoring against multiple human answers (logged with bench tag-gap).
  > an answer is deemed 100% accurate if at least 3 workers provided that exact answer.
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S3][vqa-s3]
  - why: The dataset ships train and validation answers for training, and both release papers train their VQA models (LSTM and CNN models, attention models, MCB) on train+val and score them as trained; VQA as a task is a general perception and language task, not a discipline.
  > We train on VQA train+val.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `reasoning-general/commonsense` · [S1][vqa-s1]
  - why: The paper studies which questions need commonsense, and the site says answering needs it, but the questions were collected to need the image and the score is agreement about the image; commonsense is a step towards the answer, not the scored relation.
  > These questions require an understanding of vision, language and commonsense knowledge to answer.
- `evaluation_method` not `exact-match` · [S5][vqa-s5]
  - why: The match itself is exact after normalisation, but an answer only one or two annotators gave earns one or two thirds of a point, and exact-match excludes partial credit.
  > We introduce a new evaluation metric which is robust to inter-human variability in phrasing the answers
- `evaluation_method` not `multiple-choice` · [S3][vqa-s3]
  - why: v1.0 also had a multiple-choice task with 18 candidates per question, scored by the same accuracy on the chosen candidate, so several candidates can earn credit and there is no single keyed option or stated chance baseline. v2.0 dropped the task. It is recorded as the subset vqa#multiple-choice (see review\_checks).
  > For multiple-choice task, 18 candidate answers are created for each question.

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `id`) The id. Proposed \`vqa\`, with v1.0 and v2.0 as versions, by the allocation rule that a dotted release or vN is a version of the same benchmark and only a successor its maintainers name as a new benchmark gets its own id. The maintainers call v2.0 the 2nd iteration of the VQA dataset and challenge, EvalAI's record calls v1.0 the 1st edition of the VQA dataset, and v2.0 keeps the site, team, question types, metric, splits and evaluation code. The other reading is \`vqa-v2\` as its own benchmark -- it has its own paper and title, is cited and reported as "VQAv2" on its own, re-balances rather than extends v1.0, drops the multiple-choice task and has its own test answers, and v1.0 and v2.0 scores are never compared. A third question is the generic-name rule, since VQA is also the task's name (the paper introduces the task as VQA) and the corpus already uses "VQA" for other benchmarks' tracks; a disambiguated id such as \`visualqa\` would follow it, while MATH's bare \`math\` is the precedent against. Ids are a human act; this stays a proposal. · [S15][vqa-s15]
   > as part of the 2nd iteration of the Visual Question Answering Dataset and Challenge (VQA v2.0)
2. (field `versions`) version\_kind for v2.0 is edition (new items on the same task, breaking). It reuses v1.0's real-image questions with new complementary images and answers, so revision (the same items changed) is arguable; and v1.0 is marked revision as the first release, following OSWorld's 1.0. The betas are not listed as versions. · [S18][vqa-s18]
   > The 1st edition of the VQA Challenge was organized in CVPR 2016 on the 1st edition (v1.0) of the VQA dataset
3. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method is reference-metric because exact-match excludes partial credit, but VQA accuracy is not a similarity measure like BLEU; it is an exact match against each of ten human answers, credited by how many gave it. A missing-term gap was logged; a consensus-match term, or exact-match allowing partial credit against multiple references, would fit better. · [S5][vqa-s5]
   > machine accuracies are averaged over all 10 choose 9 sets of human annotators
4. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) The human anchor (83.30% on v1.0 real-image test-standard) is from v1.0, measured by holding one annotator out against nine, and the best v2.0 test-standard rows are above it (87.85, a personal entry, and 87.07, Molmo2-8B), so it is not a ceiling for v2.0. Whether to record it as a v1.0 Baseline, treat the anchor as none-known for v2.0, or look for a v2.0 human figure not in the sources read. · [S3][vqa-s3]
   > real images (83.30%) and abstract scenes (87.49%)
5. (field `as_used`) Split reporting is uneven in the literature. The maintainers ask for test-standard, but EvalAI reveals test-dev on every submission and the validation answers are public, and recent abstracts such as JUICE's report "VQAv2" with no split. A score's split should be checked before it is compared. · [S9][vqa-s9]
   > Report test-standard accuracies, which can be calculated using either of the non-test-dev phases
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type academic-lab. The team is described only as the VQA team or Consortium, the papers' authors span Virginia Tech, Georgia Tech and others, and the repository is in the GT-Vision-Lab organisation (formerly VT-vision-lab). That the organisation is Georgia Tech's lab is read from its name, not stated; community-collective or conference-workshop are the alternatives. · [S18][vqa-s18]
   > "team\_name":"VQA Team"
7. (field `governance.independence_flags`) funded-by-evaluated-party rests on Google Faculty Research Awards in the v1.0 paper's acknowledgements and Google's PaLI-X and PaliGemma rows on the leaderboard. ### 2.4 RefCOCO (refcoco)

`data/benchmarks/multimodal/refcoco.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Referring expression comprehension on COCO photos: box the object a phrase describes (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg).*

Three datasets of referring expressions on MS-COCO photographs, used together as the standard test of referring expression comprehension. Given an image and a short English phrase that singles out one object among others of its category, a system must return that object's bounding box. RefCOCO and RefCOCO+ were collected at UNC with the ReferItGame, a two-player game in which one player writes an expression for a highlighted object and the other must click it. RefCOCO+ bans location words, so its expressions describe appearance only. RefCOCOg (Google Refexp) was written on Mechanical Turk without a game, and its expressions are longer, often whole sentences. A prediction is correct when its intersection over union with the true box is above 0.5. Accuracy is reported per split: val, testA (images with several people) and testB (images with several objects of another category) for RefCOCO and RefCOCO+, and val and test of the UMD partition for RefCOCOg. Google's own test split for RefCOCOg was never released. Every split, labels included, is public through the refer toolkit. There is no leaderboard, and results appear only in papers. The benchmark was designed for models trained on its train splits. It is now reported mostly for vision-language models that write the box as coordinates.

#### refcoco · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary multimodal/visual-grounding · [S1][refcoco-s1]
  - why: Every item is scored on whether a natural-language expression was bound to the right region of a photograph, which is visual-grounding's definition and the case multimodal's inclusion test names ("binding an expression to a region"). The box is scored by IoU, as in detection, but the target is fixed by the expression, and every image holds two or more objects of the target's category, so a category label does not resolve it. Vision's exclusion test sends exactly this case ("an expression grounded in a scene") to multimodal.
  > referring expression comprehension where the input is a natural language expression and the goal is to localize the referred object in the image
- `capability` = grounding · [S4][refcoco-s4]
  - why: The score is whether an English expression was attached to the right object in a presented photograph, which is grounding's inclusion test. Expressions were kept only when a second person could find the object from them.

### 2.5 ChartQA (chartqa)

`data/benchmarks/multimodal/chartqa.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Question answering over real-world charts, human-written and T5-generated questions, scored by relaxed accuracy.*

Questions about real-world bar, line and pie charts crawled from Statista, Pew Research, Our World in Data and the OECD. ChartQA-H holds 9,608 questions written by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, who were asked for compositional questions (at least two arithmetic or logical operations, such as a sum or a difference) and visual ones that refer to marks by colour, length or position. ChartQA-M, the augmented set, holds 23,111 questions generated by T5 models from Statista's human-written chart summaries, its test set cleaned by hand. Answers are open-vocabulary, mostly numbers. Scoring is relaxed accuracy: a numeric answer counts when it is within 5% of the gold answer, and any other answer must match exactly. Each set has a 1,250-question test split, reported separately and together. The release paper fine-tuned table-QA and vision-language models (T5, VL-T5, TaPas and its VisionTaPas extension) on the training split, with and without the chart's gold data table. General vision-language models now report the test set among many evaluations, and the maintainers' 2025 successor, ChartQAPro, describes ChartQA as showing performance saturation.

#### chartqa · Identity and id

#### chartqa · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary multimodal/chart-diagram-understanding · [S1][chartqa-s1]
  - why: Every item is a natural-language question about a chart image, and the score is whether the answer in language matches the gold answer, so the question-chart-answer correspondence is what is scored, which is multimodal's inclusion test ("answering in language about an image"); vision's exclusion test sends a question answered about an image to multimodal. chart-diagram-understanding is the leaf for questions that need reading charts. Reading the chart's printed labels and values is a step towards the answer, not a scored quantity, and many questions turn on the marks themselves rather than on any text.
  > They also commonly refer to visual features of a chart in their questions.
- `capability` = perception · [S3][chartqa-s3]
  - why: The values, labels and marks the answer depends on must be recovered from the chart image. The paper's models lose accuracy when the data table has to be extracted from the image rather than given, and visual questions refer to marks by colour, height and length.
  > This highlights the increasing challenge of automatic data extraction from real-world charts with diversity in styles.
- `capability` = quantitative-reasoning · [S3][chartqa-s3]
  - why: Crowdworkers were asked for compositional questions needing at least two operations such as sums, differences and averages, and 76.33% of 300 sampled human-written questions are compositional or both visual and compositional; most answers are numbers derived by those operations rather than read off the chart.
  > Compositional questions contain at least two mathematical/logical operations like sum, difference and average
- `evaluation_method` = numeric-tolerance-match, exact-match · [S3][chartqa-s3]
  - why: Relaxed accuracy splits by answer type. A numeric answer is correct within 5% of the gold answer, a relative tolerance the paper adopts from PlotQA to absorb data-extraction error; a non-numeric answer must match exactly. Accuracy is the share of items marked correct.
  > We consider an answer to be correct if it is within 5% of the gold answer. For non-numeric answers, we still need an exact match to consider an answer to be correct.
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S4][chartqa-s4]
  - why: The dataset ships train, validation and test splits, and the release paper's entrants are table-QA and vision-language models (T5, VL-T5, TaPas, VisionTaPas) fine-tuned on the training split for 30 epochs and scored as trained; the repository's model code trains on it.
  > In order to train the T5 model on any ChartQA dataset

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `vision/ocr-handwriting` · [S3][chartqa-s3]
  - why: Answering needs the labels, legends and values printed on the chart, and the paper's own pipeline runs text recognition inside ChartOCR to rebuild the data table, but ocr-handwriting scores a transcription and ChartQA scores no transcription. The paper measures its data extraction only as an appendix diagnostic of its pipeline, not as the benchmark's score.
  > Table 9: Accuracies of our data extraction algorithm on the test sets of DVQA, PlotQA, and ChartQA.
- `capability` not `grounding` · [S3][chartqa-s3]
  - why: Visual questions name marks by colour or position ("orange line", "tallest bar"), but the score is the final answer, not whether an expression was bound to the right mark, and no source claims grounding.
  > visual questions refer to the visual attributes such as color, height, and length of graphical marks (e.g., bars) in the chart

### 2.6 Perception Test (perception-test)

`data/benchmarks/multimodal/perception-test.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*11.6k scripted real-world videos with audio and six tasks, from point tracking to video QA, for multimodal video models.*

A diagnostic benchmark from Google DeepMind for multimodal video models: 11,609 real-world videos with audio, 23 seconds on average, filmed by about 100 crowd-sourced participants following 37 scripts the research team designed to probe memory, abstraction, physics and semantics. Six annotation types define six tasks: single object tracking (average IoU), single point tracking (average Jaccard), temporal action and temporal sound localisation (mAP over temporal IoU), multiple-choice video QA with three options (top-1 accuracy), and grounded video QA, whose answers are object tracks (HOTA). Models are meant to be evaluated zero-shot, few-shot or after limited fine-tuning on a small training split (about 20% of the videos); the validation split (about 50%) is public with its labels, and the held-out test split's labels stayed with the maintainers' evaluation servers. Yearly challenges on EvalAI ran at ICCV 2023, ECCV 2024, ICCV 2025 and ECCV 2026. From 2025 the tracks were consolidated, and the unified video QA track added 1,842 five-option questions that recast point tracking and action localisation as video QA. Each task is scored on its own. The paper's human baseline reaches 91.4% on multiple-choice QA, against 46.2% for the best zero-shot model it tested.

**Evidence** (45 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### perception-test · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][perception-test-s1]
  > a multimodal benchmark using real-world videos to help evaluate the perception capabilities of a model
- `released` = 2022-10-12 · [S1][perception-test-s1]
  > October 12, 2022 Research Measuring perception in AI models
- `release_venue` = NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks Track · [S2][perception-test-s2]
  > NeurIPS 2023) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks

#### perception-test · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary multimodal/video-language; secondary multimodal/visual-grounding, vision/video-understanding, vision/image-matching-correspondence, audio-speech/audio-event-detection-localization · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: The benchmark is built for multimodal video models, and its headline result is multiple-choice video QA, where a question and three options in text are answered about the video and its audio. What is scored is whether the answer corresponds to the video, which multimodal's inclusion test admits and vision's exclusion test sends away ("a question answered about an image"); vision/video-understanding's own distinction sends a video benchmark posed as question answering to video-language. Four of the six tasks are scored inside one modality (object and point tracking and action localisation on the video, sound localisation on the audio), so those subsets carry their own domain\_override and their leaves are secondary here, as is visual-grounding for grounded video QA, which binds a language question to object tracks. The 2025 and 2026 challenges recast tracking and localisation as multiple-choice video QA, and outside work reports the benchmark as a video QA task (V-JEPA 2).
  > Human baseline results compared to state-of-the-art video QA models show a substantial gap in performance (91.4% vs 46.2%)
- `capability` = perception · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: Every task gives the model a video with its audio and scores what it recovers from them, whether box or point tracks, labelled temporal segments, a chosen answer or answer tracks.
  > the model receives a video with audio, plus a task-specific input
- `capability` = grounding · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: Grounded video QA scores whether the object tracks a model returns are the ones a language question refers to; the question takes the place of a class label.
  > with the conditioning given as a language task or question as opposed to a class label
- `capability` = memory-retention · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: The Memory skill area asks about objects and events separated from the moment they matter by intervening footage, such as what changed on a table after the camera looked away, and the paper reports multiple-choice scores per skill area.
  > The camera is filming a table, then looks away for a few seconds, then looks back at the table.
- `capability` = temporal-reasoning · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: Action and sound localisation are scored on when segments start and end, by mAP over temporal IoU with the reference segments, the case the term's DCASE example admits; Memory questions also ask for the order in which things happened.
  > based on temporal IoU between predicted and ground truth temporal segments
- `evaluation_method` = multiple-choice, domain-metric · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: Multiple-choice video QA picks one of three supplied options, so its chance baseline is 33% (the 2025-2026 additions have five options, 20%). The other five tasks are scored by vision metrics, each on its own -- average IoU for object tracks, average Jaccard for point tracks, mAP over temporal IoU for action and sound segments, and HOTA for grounded QA's answer tracks.
  > out of which only one is correct, and the model has to pick one answer (33% random chance)
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model, task-specific-supervised-model, human-nonexpert · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: The paper's subjects are pre-trained multimodal models (Flamingo, SeViLA, GPT-4) evaluated zero-shot or few-shot or fine-tuned on the small training split, and the 2025-2026 rules admit any model, public VLM APIs included. No model then did all six tasks, so the paper's baselines are per-task models (SiamFC, TAP-Net, ActionFormer fine-tuned on the localisation classes), and the tracking and localisation tracks rank task-trained systems. The human baseline is 30 crowd-sourced participants answering 126 questions with no training, under the same protocol.
  > In principle, any model can be evaluated on our benchmark, either in a zero/few-shot setting or by fine-tuning on our limited train split.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `multimodal/audio-language` · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: Audio is an input to every task and sound localisation is scored, but no task scores a correspondence between audio and language; sounds are labelled from a fixed list of 16 classes.
  > label them from a list of 16 audio segment labels
- `capability` not `causal-reasoning` · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: Counterfactual questions exist, but they are 733 of the 38,060 multiple-choice pairs, drawn from 5 unique questions, and the paper's example turns on reordering written letters rather than on the effect of an intervention.
  > Counterfactual 733 (5)

#### perception-test · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system V-JEPA 2, aligned with an 8B language model · [S6][perception-test-s6]
  > 84.0 on PerceptionTest
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = false · [S3][perception-test-s3]
  - why: The test labels behind the challenge rankings were never released and every server that scored them has closed, so no new test score can be produced. Anyone can score the public validation split, which the paper's own baselines report.
  > An evaluation server is made available together with the videos from the held-out test split.
- `task` = exists true; input a video with its audio, 23 seconds on average, the task specification: a box or points to track, a question with three options, or a question whose answer is object tracks; output Per task -- a box track, point tracks with occlusion, labelled temporal segments of actions or sounds, one option, or a list of object tracks.; scoring Per task -- average IoU, average Jaccard, mAP over temporal IoU, top-1 accuracy or HOTA; validation is scored locally and test through the challenge servers. · [S3][perception-test-s3]

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `versions`) Identity. One entry for the benchmark, with the challenges as versions and the 2025-2026 unified additions as a subset. Tracks on other data (hour-long video QA in 2024 and 2025, KilometerVision and KilometerAudio in 2026, the 2025 interpretability and guest tracks) are left out; the 2026 challenge is half such tracks. · [S4][perception-test-s4]
   > NEW this year: KilometerVision track probing spatial intelligence in walking tour videos
2. (field `domain`) Primary domain multimodal/video-language rests on the headline task and the benchmark's framing for multimodal video models; four of the six tasks are scored inside one modality and carry vision or audio leaves through domain\_override. · [S3][perception-test-s3]
   > Human baseline results compared to state-of-the-art video QA models show a substantial gap in performance (91.4% vs 46.2%)
3. (field `subsets`) Vision has no tracking leaf. Object tracking is put under video-understanding and point tracking under image-matching-correspondence (corresponding points across frames); grounded video QA is visual-grounding with video-language secondary.
4. (field `versions`) 2023, 2024 and 2026 are recorded as non-breaking track-sets and only 2025 as an edition, on the evidence that the README lists one set of challenge video IDs; no source says outright that the 2024 tracks reused the 2023 test subsets. · [S9][perception-test-s9]
   > Since some of the challenges use subsets of the benchmark
5. (field `activity`) activity between-rounds rather than closed. Four yearly rounds ran, but no fifth is announced and the last server closed eight days before this reading. · [S5][perception-test-s5]
   > "end\_date":"2026-10-06T23:59:59Z"
6. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark rests on Flamingo, a baseline in the defining paper whose own paper shares authors with this one, not on a maintainer's challenge entry. · [S3][perception-test-s3]
   > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
7. (field `governance.submission_process`) publication-gated is not tagged. Whether the technical report is a condition of ranking or only of prizes is not stated plainly. · [S7][perception-test-s7]
   > Participants need to submit a technical report
8. (field `capability`) memory-retention and temporal-reasoning rest on the skill-area diagnostics and the localisation metric; causal-reasoning, spatial-reasoning and abstraction were rejected, although the paper names Physics and Abstraction as skill areas. Each subset's capability\_override deliberately drops the terms its task does not test (grounding outside grounded QA, memory-retention outside multiple-choice QA), which the validator warns about.
9. (field `execution.harness_availability`) harness reference-implementation-only. The notebooks compute each task's metric on validation, but the servers' test scoring code is not in the repository.
10. (field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance has crowd-authored for the labels; the research team designed the scripts and questions, which might add expert-authored.

### 2.7 Video-MME (video-mme)

`data/benchmarks/multimodal/video-mme.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-10 · last verified 2026-11-10

*2,700 four-option questions on 900 YouTube videos from 11 seconds to an hour, answered with or without subtitles.*

A video question-answering benchmark for multimodal LLMs from the Video-MME team, whose authors come from Nanjing University and seven other institutions (CVPR 2025). 900 videos with a total of 254 hours were collected from YouTube across 6 domains (Knowledge, Film & Television, Sports Competition, Artistic Performance, Life Record, Multilingual) and 30 subcategories, 300 each of short (under 2 minutes), medium (4-15 minutes) and long (30-60 minutes) videos. Annotators with research experience in vision-language learning watched each whole video and wrote three multiple-choice questions with four options, 2,700 in all, over 12 task types from perception to reasoning and synopsis; a second annotator reviewed each, and questions that Gemini 1.5 Pro could answer from the text alone were sent back for revision. The model receives sampled frames, optionally the subtitles matched to those frames (744 videos have them) or the audio, and the question, and answers with a letter; accuracy is computed by regular-expression matching with no judge model. The leaderboard reports Overall and per length accuracy without and with subtitles; in the paper Gemini 1.5 Pro led at 75.0% and 81.3%. The items and answers are public on Hugging Face under academic-use-only terms, and the maintainers score model responses e-mailed to them.

#### video-mme · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary multimodal/video-language · [S4][video-mme-s4]
  - why: Every scored item is a four-option question answered in language about a video, and the construction removed questions a model could answer from the text alone, so the score measures whether the chosen answer corresponds to the video. That is the correspondence multimodal's inclusion test takes and vision's exclusion test hands over; vision/video-understanding's distinction sends a video benchmark posed as question answering to video-language even when it calls itself video understanding, as this one does. Subtitles and audio enter only as optional inputs; nothing is scored inside one modality.
  > filter out QA pairs that can be answered solely based on the textual questions
- `capability` = perception · [S4][video-mme-s4]
  - why: The model receives sampled frames (and optionally subtitles or audio) and is scored on what it recovers from them; the task types span OCR, attribute, object and action recognition, counting and temporal perception.
  > these questions encompass 12 distinct task types, including perception, reasoning, and information synthesis
- `capability` = temporal-reasoning · [S4][video-mme-s4]
  - why: Temporal perception and temporal reasoning are among the scored task types, and the paper's worked cases need events linked across a video, such as an injury and a reappearance 24 minutes apart; the evaluation script reports accuracy per task type.
  > and long-range temporal reasoning, making them highly challenging
- `capability` = context-integration · [S4][video-mme-s4]
  - why: The video, and in the subtitle setting the matched subtitles, supply what determines the answer. Questions a strong model answered from the text alone were revised, and that model scored under 15% text-only, so the score tests whether the supplied material was used.
  > Gemini 1.5 Pro achieves less than 15% accuracy in the text-only setup
- `evaluation_method` = multiple-choice · [S4][video-mme-s4]
  - why: Each question has four options, A to D, with the correct letter near-uniformly distributed, so chance is 25% (Epoch's random baseline is 0.25). The model is told to answer with the letter only, which is extracted by regular expression and compared with the key, with no judge model.
  > each accompanied by four candidate options, contributing to a total of 2,700 QA pairs
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model · [S3][video-mme-s3]
  - why: The subjects are image and video MLLMs prompted directly, each with its own frame sampling, with the model's default multiple-choice prompt or the paper's standard one, which asks for the letter only. No tools or harness loop are involved.
  > Respond with only the letter (A, B, C, or D) of the correct option.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `vision/video-understanding` · [S4][video-mme-s4]
  - why: The paper and README frame the benchmark as video understanding, and the task types include action and object recognition, but every task is posed as a multiple-choice question, and no score is a label or a temporal segment without language to correspond to.
  > counting problems, action recognition, and temporal perception
- `domain` not `multimodal/audio-language` · [S4][video-mme-s4]
  - why: Audio is one of the benchmark's advertised input modalities, but it is an optional third setting that the paper reports for Gemini 1.5 Pro alone, because most models took no audio; the leaderboard has no audio column, and its two headline conditions are frames without and with subtitles (see review\_checks).
  > Unfortunately, most of the open-source models do not support audio input, so audio evaluation is omitted.
- `capability` not `memory-retention` · [S4][video-mme-s4]
  - why: The long subset's median certificate length is 890.7 s, so the needed evidence is spread across the video, but the whole sampled video is given at once with the question, and length alone is a property of the input, which the term's exclusion rules out. No subset isolates retention.
  > our dataset yields a median certificate length of 26s, 164.7s, and 890.7s for short, medium and long videos
- `evaluation_method` not `model-graded-judge` · [S3][video-mme-s3]
  - why: The paper and README both say no external model is used to extract or grade the answer.
  > The evaluation does not introduce any third-party models, such as ChatGPT.

A November 2026 audit of long-video QA methods runs on the full long subset, and the README records frontier model releases reporting it through December 2025. The same team's Video-MME-v2 (April 2026) argues that existing video benchmarks are saturating, but it is a separate benchmark and has not replaced this one in use (see review\_checks).
  > On the full Video-MME long bucket (n=900, K=8), no tested selector significantly improves over uniform sampling.
- `activity` = accepting-submissions · [S3][video-mme-s3]

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `lineage`) Identity. Video-MME-v2 is recorded as a separate benchmark by the same team rather than an edition, because it changes the task (eight options, a tri-level hierarchy) and the scoring (group-based non-linear) as well as the items, and is cited on its own. Same maintainer and same name stem argue for an edition; 04 S4's edition test needs the same task definition. No id was allocated for it. · [S8][video-mme-s8]
   > strategy that enforces both consistency across related queries and coherence in multi-step reasoning
2. (field `lineage`) tests/test\_overlap\_sample.py asserts that family\_key('Video-MME v2') equals family\_key('VideoMME'), treating v2 as the same family for overlap sampling, which disagrees with this entry's identity call.
3. (field `domain.secondary`) Audio. multimodal/audio-language was rejected as a secondary because audio is an optional setting reported for one model and absent from the leaderboard; the Video-MME-v2 corpus record took audio-language as a secondary for v2, where omni models are scored with raw audio. The paper's abstract lists audio among the benchmark's four key features. · [S4][video-mme-s4]
   > \3) Breadth in data modalities, integrating multi-modal inputs besides video frames, including subtitles and audios
4. (field `subsets`) The subtitle conditions are modelled as two subsets over the same 2,700 questions, as 04 S4's table names this case, though they are input conditions rather than item sets; subset\_used in the comparability profile carries the choice on claims.
5. (field `subsets`) The 12 task types (and 6 domains, 30 subcategories) are not subsets, because their item counts and the full task-type list are in a figure that was not read; 04 S6 cites "VideoMME reports 12 sub-scores" as subset material.
6. (field `versions`) The 2024-06-15 revision is marked breaking because videos were replaced and re-annotated, but the number of items changed is not stated and the leaderboard re-dated the paper's rows to that day. · [S3][video-mme-s3]
   > \*\*\`2024.06.15\`\*\* 🌟 We have refreshed our evaluation: 1) replace broken and potentially broken video links, and re-annotated them
7. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark is left unset. The paper's reference list gives the VITA papers authors who are Video-MME authors, including its project leader, but the flag would rest on comparing author lists, which the entry does not quote. Set it if a reviewer accepts that evidence; the VITA rows are baselines in the defining paper and on the maintainers' board, not e-mailed entries. · [S6][video-mme-s6]
   > VITA 1.5 Tencent Youtu Lab & NJU 7B 16 2025-01-22 56.1 58.7
8. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type community-collective rather than academic-lab. Every affiliation is academic and Nanjing University leads the project, but the repository moved from a personal account to a shared organisation account, and the data is served from LMMS-Lab's Hugging Face account.
9. (field `execution.harness_availability`) harness official-harness rests on the README naming its scoring script, which sits in a separate personal account at an unpinned main branch and was not read; reference-implementation-only may fit if the maintainers score submissions with other code.
10. (field `execution.reproducibility_blockers`) licence-restriction as a blocker, and fully-open access despite academic-only terms. The terms forbid commercial use and redistribution, while frontier developers report the benchmark (the README's news items); whether evaluation counts as commercial use is not stated. · [S3][video-mme-s3]
   > Without prior approval, you cannot distribute, publish, copy, disseminate, or modify Video-MME in whole or in part.
11. (field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance expert-authored follows the paper's "expert annotators"; their expertise is vision-language research, not the videos' subject domains, so crowd-authored may fit.
12. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle active rather than saturated or superseded. The top row is 81.6% with subtitles (no human ceiling is known), and the same team's v2 abstract says existing benchmarks are saturating, but outside papers still report Video-MME in late 2026. · [S8][video-mme-s8]
   > existing benchmarks are becoming increasingly saturated, exposing a critical discrepancy between inflated leaderboard scores and real-world model capabilities

**Evidence** (41 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### mmau · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][mmau-s1]
  > We present MMAU, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal audio understanding models on tasks requiring expert-level knowledge and complex reasoning.
- `released` = 2024-10-24 · [S1][mmau-s1]
  > Submitted on 24 Oct 2024
- `release_venue` = ICLR 2025 (Spotlight) · [S2][mmau-s2]
  > "venue":{"value":"ICLR 2025 Spotlight"}

#### mmau · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary multimodal/audio-language; secondary audio-speech/audio-event-understanding, audio-speech/music-understanding · [S3][mmau-s3]
  - why: Each item pairs an audio clip with a question and answer options in text, and the score is whether the option chosen is the correct answer about that clip. The metric is defined over the pair, so the scored quantity is the correspondence between the language answer and the audio, which audio-speech's exclusion test sends to multimodal/audio-language. The paper checks this by replacing the audio with Gaussian noise; models that keep their score are said not to be listening. audio-event-understanding and music-understanding were weighed as primaries, since a third of the items are about environmental sounds and nearly half of the information-extraction items are about music (instruments, chords, tempo, genre). Both lose because the attribute is never scored as a label recovered from the signal; it is scored only through a language answer to a language question, so they are secondary, for the sound and music thirds.
  > This progression demands that models not only perceive the audio with respect to the text prompt but also apply advanced cognitive skills to respond faithfully.
- `capability` = perception · [S3][mmau-s3]
  - why: Every item presents a raw audio clip, and the answer has to be recovered from what is heard; the paper's error analysis finds perceptual errors to be the largest share of both models' mistakes.
  > challenging models to jointly process auditory content and text, recall relevant knowledge, and engage in complex reasoning to solve the tasks
- `capability` = knowledge-recall · [S3][mmau-s3]
  - why: The protocol supplies the clip, the question and the options only. Information-extraction items are defined as needing outside world knowledge where the audio alone does not settle the answer (eco-acoustic knowledge, historical and cultural reasoning), and the benchmark claims domain-specific knowledge as part of what it tests.
  > We define an information extraction question as one that requires a deep understanding of audio, detailed content analysis, and the application of external world knowledge when necessary.
- `evaluation_method` = multiple-choice · [S3][mmau-s3]
  - why: The model is given the options and told to pick one; its answer is extracted and matched to one of the supplied options, and the score is micro-averaged accuracy. The chance baseline is about 26% (the random-guess row of the original board, 25.92% on test).
  > which is then matched to one of the provided options using string matching
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model, human-nonexpert · [S3][mmau-s3]
  - why: The models scored are chat or instruct audio-language models prompted once per question with the clip and the options; non-instruct versions are left out because they do not answer by choosing an option. Text-only LLMs given audio captions are a robustness check, not the designed subject. Eight university students answered test-mini under the same protocol, with no domain screen stated.
  > We do not evaluate non-instruct/non-chat versions of Qwen-2, Audio Flamingo, and Pengi as they fail to follow instructions and respond by selecting options.

Considered and rejected:

- `designed_for_subjects` not `human-expert` · [S3][mmau-s3]
  - why: The original board types the human row as human\_expert, but the paper describes the eight participants only as university students; no expertise in sound, speech or music is stated.
  > We recruit 8 university students for human evaluation study.

#### mmau · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system Gemini Pro v1.5 · [S3][mmau-s3]
  > Notably, even the most advanced Gemini Pro v1.5 achieves only 52.97% accuracy
- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system Step-Audio-2 (v05.15.25 leaderboard) · S6
  > "name": "Step-Audio-2", "size": "-", "type": "closed"
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · S7
  - why: Anyone can score test-mini locally with the released answers and evaluation script, and anyone can upload test predictions to the open Space, which returns accuracy without exposing the answers.
  > Evaluates uploaded JSON and returns ONLY aggregated metrics
- `task` = exists true; input an audio clip of speech, environmental sound or music (10.14 s on average), a question in English and a list of answer options; output The text of one option.; scoring Micro-averaged accuracy over the split, reported overall and for sound, music and speech, on test-mini and test separately. The paper extracts the answer with regular expressions and string matching, shuffles the options five times and keeps the most frequent choice; the Space scores one prediction per question. · [S3][mmau-s3]
  > We use micro-averaged accuracy as our evaluation metric.
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = not-independently-reproducible · S8
  - why: The test score, which the boards rank beside test-mini, can be computed only by the maintainers' scorer, because they hold the test answers. test-mini can be scored by anyone.
  > The answers and explanations for the test set questions are withheld.
- `execution.harness` = evaluation.py in the repository (string matching of each prediction against the options); the Space applies the same rule to test. · S8

1. (field `domain`) Boundary. Primary multimodal/audio-language because the score is a language answer about a clip; audio-event-understanding and music-understanding were weighed as primaries and kept as secondaries for the sound and music thirds.    > This experiment helps assess whether models are truly attending to the audio inputs or just respond using language-priors.
2. (field `versions`) Versions. MMAU-v05.15.25 is modelled as a breaking revision of the same 10,000 items, not a new benchmark, since the README says about 25% of questions and answers and 5% of the audio were changed. The release date is null; the repository's commit list (read, not cited, because every record carries personal handles) shows the data files updated on 2025-05-16, and test-mini's file edited again on 2025-05-30, 2025-06-23 and 2025-08-10 under the same version name, so frozen may be wrong. · S8
   > \~25% of Questions & Answers have been revised for improved clarity and quality
3. (field `lineage`) MMAU-Pro is treated as a separate benchmark by 04 S4 (new items, 49 skills, open-ended answers, its own paper and site) and has no id, so no lineage edge is recorded. A curator allocating it should add the successor or variant edge here. · [S12][mmau-s12]

5. The site and README describe MMAU as 12 information-retrieval and 15 reasoning types and quote Gemini 1.5 at 66.15% and Qwen2-Audio at 55.4%, while the arXiv v1 paper says 11 information-extraction and 16 reasoning tasks and 52.97% and 52.50%. The site's figures may come from the ICLR camera-ready or a later run; the entry follows the paper read. · S13

### 2.9 GenEval (geneval)

`data/benchmarks/multimodal/geneval.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-10 · last verified 2026-11-10

*553 text-to-image prompts; a COCO detector and CLIP check each image for its objects, counts, colours, positions.*

An automated benchmark for text-to-image models from the University of Washington, with the Allen Institute for AI and LAION, published in the NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks Track. Its 553 prompts are filled in from six templates with COCO object names, ten colours, the counts two to four and four relative positions: single object, two objects, counting, colours, position, and attribute binding (two objects with two different colours). A model generates four images per prompt. Each image is checked by a Mask2Former instance-segmentation model trained on COCO, which finds the prompted objects and gives their count and bounding-box positions, and, for the colour tasks, by CLIP ViT-L/14 classifying the colour of each detected object after cropping and masking out the background. An image scores 1 only if every element of the prompt was rendered, with a reason recorded when it fails. Scores are averaged per task and the six task scores averaged into the overall score. In a Mechanical Turk study of 1,200 images, the automated verdict agreed with annotators 83% of the time, against 88% between annotators. Prompts, generation and scoring code are public, and results are published only in papers. GenEval has become a standard report for image generators and unified multimodal models, with top scores near 0.9 in 2026; a December 2025 audit found its detector-based verdicts drifting below human judgment on recent models and called the benchmark saturated.

**Evidence** (45 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### geneval · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][geneval-s1]
  > we introduce GENEVAL, an object-focused framework to evaluate compositional image properties such as object co-occurrence, position, count, and color
- `released` = 2023-10-17 · [S2][geneval-s2]
  > Submitted on 17 Oct 2023
- `release_venue` = NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks Track · [S3][geneval-s3]
  > (NeurIPS 2023) Datasets and Benchmarks Track DOI: 10.52202/075280-2270

#### geneval · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary multimodal/any-to-any-generation · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: An image is generated from text and scored on whether it corresponds to the text, which is any-to-any-generation's definition. The score is defined over the image-prompt pair. The detector looks for the objects the prompt names, and its boxes and masks are checked against the prompt's count, relative position and colours, so an image is correct only if every element of the prompt was rendered. No GenEval score is computed on the image alone. Multimodal's inclusion test covers generating in one modality from another where the correspondence is scored, and vision's exclusion test sends exactly this case to multimodal.
  > GENEVAL centers around the use of an object detection model, which verifies that the generated image contains the objects specified in the text prompt
- `capability` = generation-fidelity · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: The score is whether the generated image matches a stated specification, the prompt broken into objects, counts, colours and positions, which is generation-fidelity's inclusion test (a stated specification as the target). The verdict per image is binary, but the specification is a description to be depicted, not a discrete answer checked against a key.
  > In order to produce a fine-grained verification of how well a generated image matches the description provided in the text prompt
- `evaluation_method` = model-derived-metric · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: Every verdict is computed by released scoring models acting as automated graders, not as prompted judges. A Mask2Former (Swin-S backbone) instance-segmentation model from MMDetection, trained on COCO, finds the objects at a confidence threshold of 0.3 (0.9 for counting), and its boxes give the count and the relative position. For the two colour tasks CLIP ViT-L/14 classifies each detected object's colour zero-shot among ten colours after the image is cropped to its box and the background masked grey. The detector's version and thresholds are part of the result; the taxonomy's own example for this term is GenEval.
  > we choose the best instance segmentation model available from the MMDetection toolbox \[5\], a Mask2Former \[7\] trained on MS COCO
- `designed_for_subjects` = generative-media-model · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: The entrants are text-to-image generators, and every score is a property of the images they generate for the prompts; the paper scores Stable Diffusion versions, DeepFloyd IF, SD-XL and minDALL-E, beside a CLIP-retrieval baseline of real LAION-5B images.
  > We evaluate a variety of open-source text-to-image models.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `vision/image-generation` · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: The images are generated and scored by vision models, but image-generation is scored on properties of the image itself, and GenEval scores nothing without the prompt; it defines itself against FID for exactly that. The human study's realism question was not part of the score. Under 02 S11 rule 12 a text-to-image benchmark is vision only where the prompt merely conditions generation, so neither primary nor secondary applies.
  > Metrics such as the Frechet Inception Distance \[16\] solely evaluate image quality without taking the prompt into account.
- `capability` not `instruction-following` · [S4][geneval-s4]
  - why: The GenEval paper calls the property text-to-image alignment and never claims instruction following, which 02 S4.2 requires. The Echo-4o authors call GenEval an instruction-following benchmark, a third party's framing.
  > Previous instruction-following benchmarks, such as GenEval \[20\], have been widely adopted
- `capability` not `spatial-reasoning` · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: The position task checks that two rendered objects stand where the prompt places them, from their box centroids, a fidelity check on the output rather than reasoning about space. The paper uses the phrase only for what models find hard.
  > This supports prior claims that spatial reasoning and attribute binding are difficult for T2I models
- `capability` not `compositional-generalization` · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: The paper calls its tasks compositional, and many object pairings are rare in real data, but nothing establishes that the primitives were seen in training and only their arrangement is new, as the term's test requires; the arrangements are random samples from templates.
  > would rarely appear in a real-world dataset like LAION-5B
- `evaluation_method` not `model-graded-judge` · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: No general-purpose model is prompted for a verdict; the detector and CLIP return boxes, masks and class scores that fixed rules turn into a verdict. The successors GenEval++ (GPT-4.1) and GenEval 2 (Soft-TIFA over a VQA model) use judges, which is one reason they are separate benchmarks.
  > whereas GENEVAL breaks the prompt down into correct and incorrect elements before producing a final binary score
- `evaluation_method` not `human-crowd-eval` · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: Mechanical Turk annotators labelled 1,200 images, but only to validate the automated verdicts; no published GenEval score comes from human ratings. The GenEval 2 authors' human study of GenEval outputs is likewise an audit.
  > We conduct the study through Amazon Mechanical Turk, and gather 6,000 annotations on a total of 1,200 images
- `evaluation_method` not `reference-metric` · [S1][geneval-s1]
  - why: CLIPScore appears only as the baseline the paper compares against; GenEval itself compares no output with a reference by a similarity formula.
  > GENEVAL obtains significantly greater human agreement than the CLIPScore image-text alignment metric on complex tasks

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `lineage`) GenEval 2 and GenEval++ are treated as separate benchmarks by other maintainers and given no ids (lineage\_note). Both take GenEval's name, and GenEval 2 keeps its templated design and task kinds, so a reviewer may prefer fork records once ids are allocated; neither shares GenEval's prompts, scorer or authors. GenEval 2's paper and GenEval++'s Echo-4o paper were read only for these lines; their own repositories were not. · [S8][geneval-s8]
   > we introduce a new benchmark, GenEval 2, with improved coverage of primitive visual concepts and higher degrees of compositionality
2. (field `lineage`) GenEval 2 calls its skill set a similar-but-expanded version of GenEval's (40 objects, 20 from COCO; 18 attributes; 9 relations; counts 2 to 7), which is the strongest case for treating it as GenEval's successor in the same family. It has a different maintainer and no shared items, so 04 S4 makes it a new benchmark with a lineage link either way. · [S6][geneval-s6]
   > GenEval 2 evaluates a similar-but-expanded set of skills compared to GenEval
3. (field `lineage`) GenEval++ (280 prompts, GPT-4.1 judge) is a successor by the Echo-4o authors that is cited by its own name. Whether it warrants an entry depends on uptake outside the Echo-4o paper, which was not searched. · [S4][geneval-s4]
   > GenEval++ incorporates an automated evaluator powered by GPT-4.1 and significantly increases the difficulty and compositional complexity of test instructions
4. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle stays active because GenEval is still reported in 2026. The GenEval 2 authors argue it has been saturated for over a year by human judgment, with the automated score under-crediting recent models by up to 17.7 points, so measured headroom on the automated score (top 0.91 in May 2026) understates how saturated it is. saturated is derived and cannot be hand-set; a reviewer may want the drift recorded as a contamination or validity note elsewhere. · [S6][geneval-s6]
   > showing that GenEval is effectively saturated today, and has been for over a year
5. (field `evaluation_method`) The scorer's validity is model-dependent. The detector was trained on COCO photographs, the paper reports it failing on artistic renders and merged objects, and the GenEval 2 audit finds it unreliable on recent models' images. Scores across model generations may therefore not be comparable, which no condition field records. · [S6][geneval-s6]
   > which are no longer reliable for evaluating recent T2I models
6. (field `comparability.material_extra`) Prompt rewriting before generation is now common and moves scores by several points, and current reports often do not say whether they used it (SenseNova-U1 does not). prompt\_template\_hash is the nearest condition field; a dedicated rewriting flag may be needed. · [S6][geneval-s6]
   > in addition to images generated based on rewritten prompts for the 6 of these T2I models trained with rewriting techniques
7. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type individual rests on the repository's personal-account owner (GitHub API), with academic-lab arguable on the University of Washington authorship. The README and the API record are not archived because the account is named for an author.
8. (field `governance.independence_flags`) One author lists LAION, whose LAION-5B indexes the retrieval baseline and trained the Stable Diffusion models the paper scores; no flag was set, since no LAION system is an entrant. A reviewer may judge otherwise. · [S1][geneval-s1]
   > We also compare these models against a baseline of real images from LAION-5B
9. (field `capability`) generation-fidelity is the only capability. instruction-following was rejected because the paper does not claim it, although third parties (Echo-4o) describe GenEval that way, and compositional-generalization because no held-out-arrangement claim is made.
10. (field `subsets`) Per-task prompt counts (80, 99, 80, 94, 100, 100) are stated in the subsets' notes from the paper's Table 1, whose cells the PDF text interleaves with the templates and so could not be quoted cleanly; only the 553 total is quoted.

### 2.10 Flickr30k (flickr30k)

`data/benchmarks/multimodal/flickr30k.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-10 · last verified 2026-11-10

*31,783 Flickr photos with five crowd captions each, scored as image-text retrieval (Recall@K) and captioning.*

A corpus of 31,783 photographs of everyday activities, events and scenes taken from Flickr, each described by five crowd workers, 158,915 English captions in all. It extends the same group's Flickr 8k corpus. The defining paper built it to construct a denotation graph, a hierarchy of phrases linked to the sets of images they describe, and evaluated that graph on two text-only tasks. The dataset became a standard benchmark for matching images and sentences instead. In that use, models rank the 1,000 images of a test split for each caption (text-to-image retrieval) and the test captions, five per image, for each image (image-to-text retrieval), and the score is Recall@K, the share of queries whose true match is in the top K (usually K = 1, 5 and 10). The same split, with 1,000 validation images and the rest for training, is used for captioning, scored by BLEU, METEOR and CIDEr against the five references. Results come from papers; there is no leaderboard. Most 2025 results are zero-shot, from contrastive vision-language encoders run through third-party harnesses. The data is released through a request form, for non-commercial research and teaching, and the images stay under their owners' copyright and the Flickr Terms of Use.
